title: Microsoft outage disrupts email at Laredo colleges, halts WIC services
excerpt: A Microsoft outage knocked out email at Laredo College and TAMIU and left local WIC services unavailable on Nov. 12, with the disruption still ongoing late Thursday night.
content:
A Microsoft outage disrupted email services at Laredo College and Texas A&M International University and left local WIC services unavailable on Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026, according to KGNS.

Both colleges warned students and staff that they might have trouble getting into their email while the outage continued, KGNS reported. The WIC program said its services were unavailable and posted a notice apologizing for the inconvenience, explaining that services were temporarily down because of a system outage.

People who had WIC appointments on Nov. 12 could call the WIC office to reschedule, according to KGNS.

As of late Thursday night, the outage was still ongoing, and Microsoft was working to restore services, KGNS reported. The disruption was part of a wider Microsoft Outlook outage affecting email services across the United States on Nov. 12, according to Texas Border Business.

KGNS did not report how many people were affected or how long the outage would last.

Update — November 13, 2026

The outage continued into Friday, Nov. 13, with Microsoft saying recovery was progressing in phases but capacity had not yet fully returned to normal. In a post on X at 5:28 a.m. ET, the company said recovery actions were ongoing across its Microsoft 365 infrastructure; by 6:11 a.m. ET it said it had made additional progress, with mailbox access and delayed email processing improving, though some intermittent issues could continue, USA Today reported. Downdetector recorded about 15,000 Outlook problem reports around 6 a.m. ET Friday, down from a peak of about 130,000 on Thursday, according to USA Today. Microsoft said its investigation found that a process on affected servers responsible for establishing secure connections was becoming overwhelmed, causing the servers to stop processing requests, though the company has not confirmed a definitive root cause. Microsoft executive Charles Lamanna said Friday there was no indication the outage was caused by a cyberattack, according to El País. The company has not given a timeline for full restoration. As of Friday morning, there was no local confirmation that email service had been restored at Laredo College or TAMIU or that WIC services had resumed.

Update — November 14, 2026

Microsoft confirmed on Saturday, Nov. 14, that the services affected by the global outage had fully recovered. In its final status update, the company said it had "completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions," and that the backlog of delayed email had been processed. The outage, which began Thursday, Nov. 12, lasted more than 36 hours and drew more than 7.4 million outage reports from more than 70 countries, according to Reuters. Microsoft said the incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced after a recent network change, and that it was not related to a cyberattack or to AI agents. The company said it will publish a full post-incident report once its review is complete. As of Saturday afternoon, there was still no direct confirmation that email service had been restored at Laredo College or TAMIU or that local WIC services had resumed.

Update — November 27, 2026

Microsoft has published its final post-incident report on the Nov. 12 outage, dated Nov. 20, 2026. The report says the outage was caused by a latent software defect introduced in July 2026 in the configuration of Microsoft's gateway servers, which route traffic into Microsoft 365. The defect was triggered when a Teams failover added load while some servers were offline for planned maintenance and U.S. traffic reached its daily peak; the failure then spread from server to server and region to region. At the worst point, more than 80 percent of the gateway servers for a critical North American gateway were unresponsive, according to the report as described by The Register. Microsoft said the defect affected its own gateway servers, not standard Windows installations, and found no evidence of a cyberattack.

The report also confirms that some emails never arrived. Microsoft extended its delivery retry window from 24 to 48 hours during the outage, and the company says all queued enterprise emails were eventually delivered, with none permanently lost. But some delayed messages sent to consumer mailboxes that had been inactive for more than 30 days expired, and the senders received non-delivery reports, according to Neowin and The Register. Microsoft did not say how many emails or users were affected.

The final report also disclosed disruptions that had not been reported before, including delays in Microsoft Defender for Office — the Zero-hour auto purge feature that removes malicious emails after delivery was delayed, and users had trouble opening URLs protected by Safe Links — and disruptions to Purview, Neowin reported. To prevent a repeat, Microsoft said it plans to change its traffic distribution design, isolate gateway capacity by the first quarter of 2027, and restrict Teams failovers to affected regions by the fourth quarter of 2026.

There is still no direct confirmation that email service was restored at Laredo College or TAMIU or that local WIC services resumed.
